Stark (1968: 27) considers stress in Mochica unpredictable and therefore phonemic. She nevertheless assumes that it most often occured on the penultimate syllable. Cerrón-Palomino (1995: 133-138), after going over all Mochica material available ... concludes that the stress had a fixed, antepenultimate position. new_statements.rule_in_words: Extinct language known only from written records with inconsistent diacritics; stress placement is reconstructed and disputed. Eloranta (following Hovdhaugen 2004) holds that stress fell on the root syllable, i.e. the initial syllable (roots mostly monosyllabic, suffixes unstressed, the reduced vowel <ae> never accented and prone to syncope). Cerrón-Palomino 1995 (also held by the project, pp.133-138) argues from Oré, Martínez Compañón, Brüning and Lehmann that the native pattern was 'llana o grave' (penultimate, e.g. loan costal > kóstaj), predictable and non-contrastive, though his closing sentence says 'antepenúltima'; Stark 1968 called it phonemic but mostly penultimate.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: Eloranta ch.10 (p. ~PDF 400): a handful of words with final accent in Carrera (<lapà> 'calabash container', <munà> 'mummy ancestor', <yanà> 'servant', plus <patà>) are 'not typical in Mochica at all' and taken as Quingnam/Quechua loans. Middendorf 1892:52 and Cerrón-Palomino 1995:135 fn.89: the long genitive ending -ō carries the accent and is pronounced almost as a separate word. Cerrón-Palomino: apparent proparoxytones in Lehmann/Brüning (ónceke, súpite) are due to paragogic/epenthetic vowels in the obsolescent stage; final-stressed toponyms (Etén, Monsefú) are Hispanicized.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level, reconstructed philologically from 17th-20th c. transcriptions (Oré 1607, Carrera 1644, Martínez Compañón 1780s, Middendorf 1892, Brüning, Lehmann 1929); no phrase-level description beyond Stark's remark (reported by Cerrón-Palomino p.138) that Middendorf's kumó vs. mo kúmo might show a phrase-level accent. All authors stress that the diacritics in Carrera and Middendorf primarily mark vowel quantity, not intensity.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe colonial/republican Mochica (Yunga of Trujillo-Lambayeque; Carrera 1644 = Reque variety, Middendorf 1892 = Eten variety, the last place it was spoken), glottocode moch1259, ISO omc. The language is extinct (last rememberers early-mid 20th c.); every stress claim is a philological reconstruction from inconsistent diacritics, not an observation of speech. Note the PUCP repository titles Cerrón-Palomino's book 'La lengua de Nailamp' but the printed title is 'La lengua de Naimlap'.

new_statements.quote: p. 43: "sind diese im Chimu in der Regel kurz, die meisten Hauptwörter und Verbalwurzeln sind einsilbig." p. 52 §14: "Bei Substantiven, welche auf die Konsonanten k, t, p, m, n, ch, ts endigen, besteht der Genitiv in Anfügung der Silben -är-ō. Die Endsilbe ō ist lang und trägt nicht nur den Accent, sondern wird sogar etwas getrennt ausgesprochen, als wenn das ō ein besonderes Wort wäre: aläk, der Kazike; aläk-är-ō" §15: "Auch hier ist das o am Ende der Silbe lang und trägt den Accent: ajtärr, der Hals; ajtärr-ei-ō"
new_statements.translation: p. 43: 'in Chimu these [expressions] are as a rule short; most nouns and verb roots are monosyllabic.' p. 52 §14: 'With nouns ending in the consonants k, t, p, m, n, ch, ts, the genitive consists in adding the syllables -är-ō. The final syllable ō is long and not only carries the accent but is even pronounced somewhat separately, as if the ō were a separate word: aläk, the chief; aläk-är-ō.' §15: 'Here too the o at the end of the syllable is long and carries the accent: ajtärr, the neck; ajtärr-ei-ō.'

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Mochica has an empty rule and the existing statement (Eloranta 2020 §3.9.2) reports the sources as inconsistent (Stark penult, Cerrón-Palomino antepenult, Hovdhaugen initial/root). Middendorf gives no general rule, so it neither confirms nor refutes any of the three; it adds one datum: in genitives the long final -ō is accented, and it is pronounced as if a separate word. Cerrón-Palomino 1995 (held by the project) already notes that Middendorf is silent on stress, which this reading confirms for the Lautlehre; the -ō remark on p. 52 is the one thing he does say. The 'separate word' comment makes the datum compatible with Eloranta's root-syllable accent (the -ō behavin…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No general word-stress rule is given anywhere in the Lautlehre (which treats only vowel quality, vowel length, diphthongs and consonants). The only accent statement is morphological: the genitive ending -ō (in -är-ō and -ei-ō) is long and carries the accent, and is pronounced somewhat detached, as if it were a separate word. Middendorf also notes that most nouns and verb roots are monosyllabic, so word stress is rarely at issue.
new_statements.exceptions: none; the only accent fact concerns the genitive suffix -ō. §154 p. (scan around the scanned text) mentions that yes/no questions may be marked 'bloß durch den Ton der Rede' (only by the intonation of the utterance), a phrase-level remark, not word stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Middendorf 1892 describes the last spoken variety, the Chimu/Muchik of Eten (Lambayeque), recorded in the 1880s, and adds an appendix on Chibcha (Muisca) that is a different language. Adelaar and Muysken 2004 §3.4 (not opened) would draw on the colonial Carrera 1644 grammar and the later sources.
